initial_assessment: Synthetic educational case (bundle security tag HTEST). A 34-year-old man (DOB 1992-06-01) with about 1 week of headache and vomiting (recorded 2026-10-16; onset approximately 2026-10-09) and ECOG 2 on 2026-10-16. MRI brain 2026-10-17: well-circumscribed, lobulated, extra-axial/cortically based left frontal mass measuring 4.2 x 3.5 x 3.0 cm. MRI spine 2026-10-17: a 5 mm lobulated, intensely and uniformly enhancing posterior pial nodule at C6 with cord of normal caliber, described as imaging-suspected spinal drop metastasis and not biopsied. Image-guided stereotactic needle biopsy of the left frontal mass on 2026-10-19. The neuropathology conclusion (issued 2026-10-21) is 'suggestive of an intracranial mesenchymal tumor with spinal drop metastasis; entity not established on the current material'. Working impression: a provisional, histologically and molecularly unclassified intracranial mesenchymal neoplasm of uncertain behavior (ICD-10 D43.0), with a possible pial spinal lesion of uncertain nature (D43.4). This is not a confirmed diagnosis. Grade, molecular class, and whether the C6 nodule is metastatic or a separate lesion are all unknown; both Condition resources are provisional by design. Discrepancy to reconcile: the pathology conclusion states 'with spinal drop metastasis', but the C6 lesion was not sampled, and the C6 Condition itself states 'not biopsy-confirmed'; the pathology wording should be clarified with the pathologist before it is carried forward as fact. Both Conditions use the mCODE primary-cancer-condition profile, which does not yet capture whether the C6 lesion is secondary to the frontal mass. Prognosis and treatment cannot be framed until classification and grade are known. Until then, treat the tumor as potentially aggressive; the priorities are safety, symptom control, staging, and diagnosis rather than disease-directed therapy.
diagnostic_confirmation_and_staging: The diagnosis is not established. Confirmation requires the full neuropathology report and further tissue work-up. (1) Pathology review at tumor board: obtain the full synoptic report with histologic description (cellularity, growth pattern, pleomorphism), mitotic count, necrosis, Ki-67 index, a WHO CNS 2021 grade or an explicit statement that grade cannot be assigned, and an inventory of remaining tissue (FFPE blocks, unstained slides, any frozen or fresh tissue reserved). (2) Immunohistochemistry to exclude mimics rather than to force a subtype: STAT6 (nuclear, to screen for NAB2::STAT6 solitary fibrous tumor/hemangiopericytoma); SMARCB1/INI1 (rhabdoid and some sarcomas); melanocytic markers (SOX10, S100, Melan-A, HMB-45); lymphoid markers (CD45, CD20, CD3); germ cell markers (SALL4, OCT3/4, PLAP); epithelial markers (AE1/AE3, EMA). (3) Molecular: DNA methylation profiling against the CNS tumor classifier; RNA-based fusion sequencing for mesenchymal and sarcoma fusions (NAB2::STAT6, FET-family::CREB fusions, NTRK, MUSTN1, round-cell sarcoma fusions); DNA panel sequencing (including CDKN2A/B, TP53, RB1, BRAF). Confirm whether these were performed, are pending, failed, or were not sent. (4) What would change management: an NTRK fusion would open a targeted-therapy option; a NAB2::STAT6 result would classify the tumor as a meningeal solitary fibrous tumor/hemangiopericytoma, where surgery and radiotherapy are central and spinal dissemination is recognized; a FET-family::CREB fusion would define a different intracranial mesenchymal entity with grade-dependent management; a melanocytic lineage would shift the work-up to melanoma pathways (BRAF testing, immunotherapy); a lymphoid or germ cell lineage would change treatment fundamentally; carcinoma or SMARCB1 loss would redirect the work-up. (5) C6 lesion: establish whether it is metastatic from the frontal mass or a separate lesion. Do not biopsy the cervical pial nodule unless the tumor board judges the risk-benefit favorable, since pial cervical biopsy is high risk; CSF cytology and CSF molecular testing may be an alternative source. (6) Extent of disease: gadolinium MRI of the brain and the complete spine (cervical, thoracic, lumbar, with post-contrast imaging) to assess mass effect, edema, dural attachment, ventricular involvement, leptomeningeal enhancement, and additional lesions. The current spine report describes only the C6 lesion. No post-biopsy imaging to exclude hemorrhage is documented. (7) CSF: opening pressure, cytology, and flow cytometry, performed only after MRI excludes obstructive hydrocephalus and a lumbar block, with timing agreed with neurosurgery (post-resection CSF is an option). (8) Exclude a primary outside the CNS: CT chest, abdomen and pelvis, or whole-body PET-CT; full skin and ophthalmologic examination; testicular examination with ultrasound if abnormal; serum LDH, AFP, and beta-hCG. (9) Genetic counseling only after pathology defines an entity with a possible hereditary association (for example TP53, NF1, RB1).
immediate_management_plan: No disease-directed treatment now: no chemotherapy, no targeted therapy, no definitive radiotherapy, and no empiric regimen for an unclassified tumor. The immediate plan is safety, symptom control, staging, and multidisciplinary review. (1) Within 24-48 hours: in-person neurological examination with fundoscopy, cranial nerves, visual fields, motor and sensory testing, gait, cord-level findings, bladder and bowel function, and cognition, with a documented baseline and an updated KPS and ECOG (the last ECOG predates the biopsy and pathology). Ask specifically about seizures and red-flag symptoms. Signs of raised intracranial pressure (papilledema, drowsiness, persistent vomiting, worsening headache), a new focal deficit, new cord signs, seizure, or hydrocephalus mean same-day admission and urgent neurosurgical review. (2) Corticosteroids: if the mass is symptomatic with peritumoral edema, start dexamethasone at the lowest effective dose with gastric protection and glucose monitoring, tapering as tolerated. If lymphoma has not been excluded, discuss with neuropathology first, because steroids can reduce the diagnostic yield of later tissue. (3) Seizures: none documented. Routine prophylactic antiseizure medication is not indicated; treat any seizure promptly, with agent choice made by neurology. (4) Symptom control: antiemetic (check QTc if ondansetron is used), acetaminophen first for headache, avoid sedating drugs that would obscure the neurological examination, and maintain hydration and electrolytes. (5) Imaging: repeat MRI brain with contrast to assess post-biopsy hemorrhage and interval change for procedural planning, and a full-length spine MRI if not already performed. (6) C6 pial nodule: no myelopathy is documented, so no urgent radiotherapy or surgery is indicated on current data. Serial neurological examination; urgent MRI and neurosurgical review for any new deficit. (7) Definitive-surgery decision: neurosurgery and neuro-oncology to decide between open resection (diagnostic tissue and debulking, if judged resectable with acceptable deficit risk) and continued observation with or without repeat sampling. This requires functional mapping (fMRI or tractography) because the relationship to speech and motor cortex is not documented. (8) Radiation oncology: consult for planning awareness only. No radiotherapy before classification, grade, extent, and resectability are established. (9) Clinical trial screening once classification is known. (10) Fertility: offer sperm banking counseling before any gonadotoxic therapy is considered. (11) Supportive care: palliative care referral in parallel with diagnosis for symptom and goals-of-care support; social work; neuropsychology baseline; counseling on driving restriction and fall precautions per local law. (12) Communication: explain to the patient that the diagnosis is provisional and that the next steps are diagnostic. (13) Follow-up: tumor board re-review within 1-2 weeks, or sooner when the pathology addendum or molecular results return and after any procedure. Give written return precautions for headache, vomiting, drowsiness, seizures, weakness, gait or bladder change, and visual loss.

Specimen adequacy: amount of tissue obtained, tissue remaining, whether frozen or fresh tissue was reserved, and any frozen-section result.
Basis for the pathology phrase 'with spinal drop metastasis', given that the C6 lesion was not biopsied and its Condition is recorded as not biopsy-confirmed.

Full brain MRI report: enhancement pattern, edema, mass effect, midline shift, ventricular involvement, dural tail, venous sinus relationship, leptomeningeal enhancement, diffusion and perfusion findings, and comparison with prior imaging.
Full spine MRI report: thoracic and lumbar findings (only the cervical lesion is described), cord signal, cauda equina, and any other pial or subarachnoid lesions.
Post-biopsy imaging or CT excluding hemorrhage, and any biopsy complications.
Extracranial staging: no CT chest, abdomen, or pelvis, PET, skin or ophthalmologic examination, testicular examination, LDH, AFP, or beta-hCG results are documented.
CSF evaluation: no opening pressure, cytology, flow cytometry, or CSF molecular data; no documented decision on timing of lumbar puncture.

Laboratory data: none documented. Needed: CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, renal function (before gadolinium), coagulation studies, glucose, and infectious serologies required before any future systemic therapy.
Current full neurological examination and vital signs, including fundoscopy and papilledema status.
Seizure history and current or prior use of corticosteroids or antiseizure medication.
Current KPS and an updated ECOG. The ECOG of 2 was recorded on 2026-10-16, before the biopsy and pathology.
Past medical history, prior cancers (including any prior melanoma or sarcoma), prior radiotherapy, current medications, allergies (including contrast), and comorbidities.
Family history of cancer or hereditary tumor syndromes.
Neurosurgical assessment of resectability, extent, eloquence, and functional mapping. Radiation oncology opinion is also absent.
Symptom onset date and trajectory: only 'about 1 week' is recorded, so the exact onset date is uncertain.
Patient goals, treatment preferences, decision-making capacity, social support, and fertility wishes.
Whether a second pathology opinion or reference review has been requested for the mesenchymal classification, and the identity of the reporting pathologist.
